newsitem.title: UK: Governments seek to predict unpredictable quakes.
newsitem.headline: Governments seek to predict unpredictable quakes.

text.p: Lightning, nervous dogs and water temperature all offer hints, but scientists admitted on Thursday they were still a long way from being able to predict when and where an earthquake will hit.
Earthquake experts from all around the world were meeting to swap notes in London on Thursday and Friday but said efforts so far were discouraging.

"There has been little progress in over 25 years of research into earthquake prediction, where we use prediction in the classical sense of specifying the magnitude, time and place," Stuart Crampin, a professor of geology and geophysics at the University of Edinburgh, said.
"Indeed large earthquakes seem likely to be statistically unpredictable."
Dr Russ Evans of the British Geological Survey told delegates that governments often backed prediction schemes that had little evidence to support them.
Evans believes governments and people have been conditioned to wrongly believe that science can solve almost any problem.
"Many people adopt the view that it is only a matter of allocating suitable resources, and a solution will appear."

Despite the current scientific evidence, the Japanese government is spending hundreds of millions of yen (millions of dollars) annually in an attempt to be able to pinpoint when the next tremor will hit the earthquake-prone country.

According to Japanese official statistics, the giant quake that devastated the western port city of Kobe and surrounding areas in January 1995 wiped out about 9.6 trillion yen ($100 billion) or 0.8 percent of Japan's wealth.

The January 17 earthquake, which killed more than 6,000 people, was Japan's worst natural disaster in the postwar period. The damage was relatively small compared to that caused by the 1923 Tokyo quake, which caused losses of 10.5 percent of the nation's wealth, according to Japanese goverment statistics.

Dr Yukio Fujinawa of Japan's Research Institute for Science and Disaster Prevention said research must continue as long as there was even a remote chance of success. Some quakes can be predicted, but not consistently.
"In China, scientists have several times made earthquake predictions," Fujinawa told Reuters. "We must gather more information and hope that we will be able to mitigate these disasters."
Some studies have indicated that animals can sense quakes somehow, while water temperature and stresses in the Earth's crust can also be used as indicators.
In Japan, one of the most unstable built-up seismic regions in the world, Fujinawa and his fellow researchers have noticed that lightning storms often take place prior to an earthquake.
But with only a few years of data on this particular phenonemon, he said it was far too early to say lightning could be an early sign of a major disaster.
"There just is not enough evidence," he said.
